extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, copyholders, and other book-publishing professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing manuscripts, setting type, proofreading, and page make-up for books and printed matter; includes typographic rules, manuscript handling, proof procedures, and marks for proofreaders and copyholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation and alignment of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Indent according to rhymes and length of lines. In blank verse, where the lines are approximately of the same length, they should be aligned. If consecutive lines rhyme, they should likewise, as a rule, be aligned. If the rhymes alternate, or follow at certain intervals, indent the rhyming lines alike; that is, if, e.g., lines 1 and 3, and 2 and 4, rhyme, set the former flush in the measure previously determined by the longest line, and indent the latter (usually one em); follow this scheme in any similar arrangement. If any line is disproportionately short — that is, contains a smaller number of feet — indent it more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided in the text illustrate centering and indenting patterns for different rhyme schemes and line lengths; when quotations from different poems vary slightly in length of verse lines, indent all alike; when aligning, give the whole a centered appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for plain paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter 'plain paragraphs' are always preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where it is desired to bring into relief the opening word or words of a paragraph, or the number introducing such paragraph, or where a center-head makes more than three lines, 'hanging indention' is often employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hanging indention
rubrics_metrics.description: A hanging paragraph ('hanging indention') has the first line set flush, and the others indented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hanging indention to bring out the opening word(s) or a numbered paragraph, or when a center-head makes more than three lines (see examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads and slug usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type; the ordinary (standard) lead is 2 points thick. A slug is a strip of metal, thicker than a lead, used in make-up of printed matter — standard sizes are 6 and 12 points (a nonpareil and a pica).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter with leads between the lines is called leaded; without, solid. Nearly all books are set leaded; illustrations clarify usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center-head formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: A center 'head is a headline placed at equal distances from both margins of the page or column. Center-heads are usually set in caps or in small caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a center-head makes more than one line, either the (inverted) 'pyramid' form (for two or three lines) or 'hanging indention' (for more than three lines) is employed; examples shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-head formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: A side-head is a headline placed at the side of the page or column. It may be set in a separate line (usually set flush) or run in (run together with the paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The run-in form is more common. Side-heads are most frequently set in italics, only the first word and proper names being capitalized; sometimes in caps and small caps or in bold-face. Several example formats are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut-in head definition and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A cut-in head is a head placed in a box cut into the side of the type-page, usually set in different type, and as a rule placed under the first two lines of the paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations and cross-references (see 281) clarify placement and type choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box-head for tables
rubrics_metrics.description: A box-head is a head for a column in a ruled table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See table guidance (cross-ref to 250) for how to set box-heads in tabular material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running-heads (page headers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A running-head is a headline placed at the top of each page of a book, usually giving the main title of the work on the left-hand (verso) page, and the title of the chapter or subdivision on the right-hand (recto) page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good working rule is to set running-heads in roman or italic capitals two sizes (points) smaller than the type of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of paragraphs (plain vs hanging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of paragraphs are distinguished — plain and hanging. A plain (or regular) paragraph has the first line indented, and the others set flush; a hanging paragraph has the first line set flush and the others indented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain paragraphs for ordinary reading matter; employ hanging indention for special emphasis or layout needs (see earlier entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of different proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Galley-proof: impression of the type contained in a galley. Page-proof: impression of the type material made up into page-form. Plate- or foundry-proof: proof taken immediately before an electrotype cast with a black border. Foul proof: a galley-proof containing author's corrections. Revise: a new proof corrected from a marked proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most publications are printed from plates, not directly from type; distinctions matter for proofreading and cost implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The arranging into page-form of type-lines is called the make-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related items on leads, slugs, and proofs; make-up decisions affect pagination and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page-numbering (folio) conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A folio is a page-number. Even numbers are placed on the verso; odd, on the recto. A drop-folio is a page-number placed at the bottom of a page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow folio conventions consistently during pagination and indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript preparation: physical requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be either typewritten or in a perfectly clear handwriting (the former preferable). Sheets should be of uniform size (9"x11" desirable). Only one side of the paper should be used. Never roll manuscripts; place them flatly in a box or an envelope. The sheets should not be fastened together except by pins or clips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one piece of a page is to be fastened to another, use mucilage, not pins. Liberal margins should be left at the top and left-hand side for reader/printer directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript pagination and insert/omit notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pages should be numbered consecutively. Inserted and omitted pages should be clearly indicated: sheets to be inserted after p. 4 should be marked '4A', '4B', etc.; sheets omitted between p. 4 and p. 8 should be indicated by numbering p. 4, '4-7.' Additions to original pages should be placed after the sheets to which they belong, and should be marked 'Insert A,' 'Insert B,' etc.; indicate insertion points in the original by writing 'Here insert A' on the margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear marking avoids misplacement of slips and confusion during make-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph and footnote marking in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs should be plainly indicated, either by indenting the first line or by a ¶ mark. Footnotes should be clearly designated, either by separating them from the text by running a line across the page, or by using ink of different color. The word in the text carrying the note should be followed by a superior figure corresponding to that preceding the note. Footnotes should never be run into the text in manuscripts, whether in parentheses or otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number footnotes consecutively through an article or by chapters in a book, but be aware of linotype resetting issues: changing a single number may require resetting entire lines and subsequent notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading: timeliness and standard marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and return your proofs promptly. In marking proof-sheets, use the standard proofreaders' marks. Be careful to answer all queries in the proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays and errors often result from not attending to queries. Use standard marks (see proofreader's marks section) rather than inventing a personal system, which may confuse compositors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize late changes and avoid plate corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that changes in the type cost money. The omission or addition of a word in the middle of a paragraph may necessitate resetting the whole line and could involve repaging the entire article or chapter. Corrections in plates should be studiously avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make your manuscript as perfect as possible before delivering it to the printer. Any necessary alterations should be made in the galley-proof; each succeeding stage adds to the cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return and track proof sets and original manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: The original manuscript should in each instance be returned with the galley-proof, in order that the proof-reader may refer to it; and each successive set of proofs returned should be accompanied by the previous marked set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assists in calculating the cost of alterations properly chargeable to the author and prevents loss of information during successive proof stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreader responsibilities and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Read everything as if you yourself were the author. Be particularly careful about proper names and figures. If the copy is not perfectly clear, or if you have reason to doubt its correctness, look it up, or query it to the author. Be discreet about your queries; do not stultify yourself by asking foolish questions. Do not follow copy blindly; follow copy only when, and as far as, it is correct. Whether or not it is correct, you are the judge. Do not ask authors or editors to decide questions of style — the Manual of Style is primarily meant for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors' or editors' approval does not relieve the proofreader of responsibility. Never hesitate to correct anything palpably wrong even if the copy asserts the contrary. Cultivate speed, but accuracy is more important. In unavoidable rushes, protect yourself by noting limits and disclaiming further responsibility. Put your initial at the top of every galley you read or revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactions with copyholders
rubrics_metrics.description: In asking questions of authors or editors, make your point clear. Queries in the manuscript should be transferred to the proof, or attention should be directed in the proof to the queries made by the copy-reader in the manuscript. Do not permit yourself to be stampeded. If you think you have cause to doubt the copyholder's reading, investigate for yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not suggest to the copyholder the reading of a word or phrase which she has difficulty making out from the manuscript. If she cannot decipher the manuscript, remember that you are the arbiter. Cultivate knowledge of the 'personal equation' of the individuals you work with; adapt query style accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyholder best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a low, soft, clear reading voice. Small words are as essential as the big ones — get them all in and get them in right. Do not keep guessing at a word; look at it closely, consider the context, and do not speak it until you have made it out. Sit at right angles to your reader if possible. Give your reader a chance to make corrections; slow up the moment he puts his pencil to the paper. Evolve your own system of signals. Do not waste time over matters of style; the proofreader is supposed to know the rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a code for indicating typesetting features (e.g., tapping the table for italics) that need not be intelligible to others. Be careful in transferring marks — a mark in the wrong place means two errors uncorrected in place of one corrected. Arrange copy and proof-sheets neatly and consecutively. Never send out proofs for the first time without consulting the job ticket for the number wanted and the recipient's name and address. The manuscript should accompany the galley-proof; the foul proof should accompany the page-proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-room housekeeping and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that you are the housekeeper of the proof-room, and take pride in its neat and orderly appearance. Keeping the records, files, etc., naturally devolves upon you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect your system so that everything can be located at a moment's notice. Return every evening to the file or the bookcase any volume taken out for reference during the day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standard proofreader's marks
rubrics_metrics.description: In marking proofs use the standard proofreaders' marks: e.g., Put in CAPITALS; Put in SMALL CAPITALS; Put in lowercase; Put in italics; Put in bold face type; Delete or take out; Letter reversed; Indent / Make a new paragraph; Put in space; Close up; Bad spacing — space more evenly; Wrong font; Transpose; Carry to the left/right; Elevate; Depress; Imperfect letter — correct; Space shows between words — shove down; Straighten crooked line; Restore or retain words crossed out; Print as a logotype; Words omitted from or in copy; Query to author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt a system of your own — even if plain to you it may not be to the compositor. Use the conventional marks listed and follow their meanings precisely; a sample list is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering and handling of footnotes with linotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Number footnotes consecutively through an article or by chapters in a book; however, in matter set on the linotype machine the slightest change necessitates the resetting of the whole line. The change by omission or addition of one single number involves resetting the whole first line of each succeeding note to the end of the series, as well as the line in the text bearing the reference to the note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of machine-specific constraints: the difficulty is not met with in matter set on the monotype machine or by hand, where changing a number is simply substituting one figure for another.
